seoDescription: Hit by an uninsured or underinsured driver in Michigan? Your own UM/UIM coverage may pay, but the policy’s deadlines and conditions can void it. ATLAW explains how. Free review.
h1: Michigan Uninsured & Underinsured Motorist Claim Lawyer
tagline: About one Michigan driver in five has no insurance. The policy that protects you from them is your own, and it has rules.
secondaryKeywords: hit and run uninsured motorist michigan

c.v: The driver who hit you had no insurance, or had the $50,000 minimum and your injuries are worth far more. In Michigan that is not unusual. The state’s insurance department estimated that one driver in five was uninsured before the 2019 reform, and in Detroit the estimate was three in five. Michigan also lets drivers carry as little as $50,000 in liability coverage. The protection against both problems is uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage, UM and UIM, which you buy on your own policy and claim from your own insurer.

That claim is not automatic. UM/UIM is optional in Michigan, so the first question is whether you have it. It is a contract, so the policy’s notice deadlines, consent-to-settle clause, and shortened time limits control, and Michigan courts enforce them as written. And your own insurer, once you make the claim, defends it the way the at-fault driver’s insurer would have. This page explains how UM and UIM work in Michigan, how a UIM payment is calculated, the conditions that void claims, what happens in a hit-and-run, and what your options are against the uninsured driver personally.

ATLAW is a personal injury firm in Dearborn. sections.heading: What UM and UIM coverage are, and why Michigan makes them optional

c.v: Michigan’s no-fault law requires every policy to carry personal injury protection, property protection, and residual liability coverage (MCL 500.3101, 500.3009). It does not require uninsured or underinsured motorist coverage. Insurers offer both as optional endorsements, and many drivers decline them to save a few dollars a month without understanding what they decline.
Uninsured motorist (UM) coverage

items.v: pays what the at-fault driver’s liability insurance would have paid if the driver had none: your pain and suffering and the economic losses no-fault does not cover. It also applies, under most policies, to hit-and-run crashes where the driver is never identified.

c.v: Underinsured motorist (UIM) coverage

items.v: pays when the at-fault driver has insurance but the limits are lower than your UIM limits and lower than your damages. It fills the gap, up to your UIM limit.

c.v: Both are on your own policy, or on a policy of a relative you live with, or on the policy covering the car you were in. If you have none of those, you have no UM/UIM claim, and your options are the no-fault benefits described next and a claim against the uninsured driver personally.

sections.heading: How no-fault fits: PIP first, UM/UIM for the rest

c.v: Whatever the at-fault driver’s insurance, your medical bills, 85% of wage loss (up to $7,455 a month for crashes on or after October 1, 2026), replacement services, and attendant care are paid as no-fault PIP benefits by your own insurer, a household insurer, or, if there is none, the Michigan Assigned Claims Plan (MCL 500.3107, 500.3114, 500.3172). The at-fault driver’s lack of insurance does not affect your PIP benefits.

What it affects is everything PIP does not pay: pain and suffering, wage loss above the monthly cap or beyond three years, and medical expenses above your PIP limit. Those come from the at-fault driver’s liability policy when there is one, and from your UM/UIM coverage when there is not enough. The Assigned Claims Plan pays PIP benefits only; it does not pay pain and suffering. Our

sections.heading: When an uninsured motorist claim applies

c.v: The at-fault driver had no insurance.

items.v: Michigan requires proof of insurance to register a car, but policies lapse, and the 2024 crash reports show it. The police report’s insurance field, a letter from the driver’s listed insurer, and a Secretary of State record establish “uninsured.”

c.v: Hit-and-run.

items.v: Most policies cover a crash caused by an unidentified vehicle, with conditions: a prompt police report, and often “physical contact” between the vehicles. Michigan courts have read physical contact to include indirect contact, such as an object propelled by the fleeing vehicle, but a swerve-to-avoid crash with no contact fails under many policies.

c.v: current case law on physical-contact clauses

items.v: Report the crash to police immediately, and note anything that touched your car.

c.v: The at-fault driver’s insurer denies coverage or is insolvent.

items.v: A policy rescinded for misrepresentation, or an insurer in liquidation, can turn an insured driver into an uninsured one. Policy definitions differ on this.

sections.heading: When an underinsured motorist claim applies, and how it is calculated

c.v: UIM applies when the at-fault driver’s liability limit is less than your UIM limit and less than your damages. The calculation is a subtraction, and the policy language decides what is subtracted.
Example: you carry $250,000 in UIM coverage. The at-fault driver carries Michigan’s $50,000 minimum. Your damages are $400,000.

items.v: You recover the at-fault driver’s full $50,000 limit (policies require you to exhaust it).
Your UIM insurer owes your damages up to your UIM limit, minus the at-fault driver’s limit: $250,000 − $50,000 = $200,000 available.
Total recovered: $250,000. The remaining $150,000 is uncompensated unless another policy (the car owner’s, your employer’s, a second household policy) applies.

c.v: Two consequences people learn too late. If your UIM limit equals the at-fault driver’s limit, say $50,000 and $50,000, your UIM coverage pays nothing. And if the policy subtracts the at-fault limit from the UIM limit (a “limits-to-limits” policy) rather than from your damages, buying $100,000 in UIM against a minimum-limits driver yields $50,000 at most. The declarations page and the UIM endorsement answer these questions, and we read both in the first week.

A UM/UIM policy pays what you are “legally entitled to recover” from the at-fault driver, and most Michigan policies write the no-fault threshold into the coverage: pain and suffering is recoverable only for death, permanent serious disfigurement, or a serious impairment of body function (MCL 500.3135). Comparative fault applies as well, so a recovery is reduced by your share of fault and barred above 50% (MCL 600.2959). The policy language controls.

sections.heading: The policy conditions that void UM/UIM claims

c.v: Michigan treats an insurance policy as a contract and enforces its terms as written. The Michigan Supreme Court has held that a one-year limitation period written into a UM policy is enforceable (Rory v Continental Insurance Co, 2005) and that Michigan does not apply a “reasonable expectations” doctrine to rescue insureds from clear policy language (Wilkie v Auto-Owners, 2003). The conditions that end claims:

rows.v: Written notice of the UM/UIM claim within the period the policy sets, sometimes 30 days, sometimes “as soon as practicable”
Treating the crash as the other driver’s problem and notifying your own insurer months later
The UIM insurer’s written consent before you accept the at-fault driver’s limits and sign a release
Signing the at-fault insurer’s release to get the $50,000 quickly; the UIM insurer’s subrogation right is destroyed and the UIM claim with it
Recovery of the at-fault driver’s full policy limit before UIM pays
Settling for less than the limit
Suit or arbitration demand within the policy’s period, often one to three years from the crash
Assuming the three-year statute applies to the UM claim
Contact with the unidentified vehicle; report to police within the period set, often 24 hours
No report, or a no-contact swerve crash
Recorded statement, examination under oath, medical authorizations, independent medical examination
Refusing what the policy allows the insurer to require
Disputes decided by arbitration rather than a jury, under the procedure the policy sets
Filing in the wrong forum, or past the demand deadline
PIP benefits paid, workers’ compensation, and amounts from other policies subtracted as the policy provides
Expecting the full limit when the policy subtracts no-fault benefits

c.v: Each of these is in the policy, and each is read in the first week of a UM/UIM case. A lawyer who handles the claim against the at-fault driver without reading the client’s own policy can settle the first claim in a way that ends the second.

sections.heading: Your own insurer is the opposing party

c.v: Once you make a UM/UIM claim, your insurer “stands in the shoes” of the at-fault driver. It will argue that the other driver was not at fault, that you were, that your injury does not meet the threshold, and that your treatment was unrelated. Expect the same adjusting tactics an opposing insurer uses: a recorded statement early, an independent medical examination, and an offer calibrated to the cost of arbitration.

Michigan gives you one specific lever. Under the Uniform Trade Practices Act, a claim not paid within 60 days after the insurer receives satisfactory proof of loss bears 12% penalty interest, and the Michigan Supreme Court has held that for a UM/UIM insured, unlike a third-party claimant, the insurer owes that interest even when it reasonably disputed the claim (MCL 500.2006(4); Nickola v MIC General Insurance, 2017). On a $200,000 UIM claim paid two years late, that is $48,000. Michigan does not recognize a separate bad-faith lawsuit against a first-party insurer; the penalty interest and the contract are the remedies.

Michigan’s no-fault law abolishes most lawsuits against insured drivers, but the abolition applies only to drivers who carried the required insurance (MCL 500.3135(3)). An uninsured at-fault driver has no such protection: they can be sued personally for all of your damages, including pain and suffering without the serious impairment threshold and vehicle damage beyond the $3,000 mini-tort limit.

The obstacle is collection. Most uninsured drivers are uninsured because they could not afford insurance, and a judgment against them is paid slowly or not at all. Two tools help: Michigan suspends the driver’s license of a person who fails to pay a judgment arising from a motor vehicle crash (MCL 257.512, 257.513), which motivates payment plans, and a judgment can be renewed and enforced against wages and assets for years. Whether to pursue the driver personally is a judgment call made with the client, after the UM/UIM and no-fault claims are secured.

sections.heading: What a Michigan UM/UIM claim is worth

c.v: The recovery is the same category of damages you would have recovered from an insured at-fault driver: pain and suffering, loss of enjoyment of life, disfigurement, and economic losses PIP does not cover, up to your UM/UIM limit, less the setoffs the policy provides. The ceiling is the limit you bought, which is why the declarations page is the first document we ask for. Beyond the limit, recovery depends on other policies and on the uninsured driver’s assets.

faqs.question: Is uninsured motorist coverage required in Michigan?

answer.v: No. Michigan requires PIP, property protection, and liability coverage (MCL 500.3101, 500.3009). UM and UIM are optional. Check your declarations page; if it does not list them, you do not have them.

faqs.question: I was hit by an uninsured driver. Who pays my medical bills?

answer.v: Your own no-fault insurer, or a household member’s, or the Assigned Claims Plan if there is none. PIP benefits do not depend on the other driver’s insurance. UM coverage is for pain and suffering and the losses PIP does not cover.

faqs.question: What is the difference between uninsured and underinsured coverage?

answer.v: UM applies when the at-fault driver has no insurance or cannot be identified. UIM applies when the driver has insurance but less than your UIM limit and less than your damages.

faqs.question: How much will my UIM policy pay?

answer.v: Your UIM limit minus the at-fault driver’s liability limit, up to your damages, under most Michigan policies. $250,000 in UIM against a $50,000 driver leaves $200,000 available. If your UIM limit equals the other driver’s limit, UIM pays nothing.

faqs.question: Can I settle with the other driver’s insurer first?

answer.v: Not without your UIM insurer’s written consent. Most policies require it, and Michigan courts enforce the requirement. Settling without consent can void the UIM claim.

faqs.question: The driver fled. Do I have a claim?

answer.v: Under most policies, yes, if you reported the crash to police promptly and the policy’s physical-contact condition is met. Your no-fault benefits come through your own policy or the Assigned Claims Plan regardless.

faqs.question: Do I have three years to make a UM claim?

answer.v: Not necessarily. The three-year statute applies to the lawsuit against the driver. The UM/UIM claim is governed by the policy, and Michigan courts have upheld one-year contractual periods (Rory v Continental, 2005). Read the policy.

faqs.question: Will my rates go up for using my own UM coverage?

answer.v: Michigan law prohibits insurers from raising rates or refusing renewal based on a claim for which you were not at fault (MCL 500.2118(2)(a)).

c.v: citation

faqs.question: Can I sue the uninsured driver?

answer.v: Yes. An uninsured driver has no no-fault tort immunity (MCL 500.3135(3)) and can be sued for all damages. Collection is the practical problem; a license suspension for an unpaid judgment (MCL 257.512) is one tool.

faqs.question: My insurer is delaying my UIM claim. What can I do?

answer.v: After 60 days from satisfactory proof of loss, the claim bears 12% penalty interest (MCL 500.2006(4)), and under Nickola v MIC (2017) the insurer owes it even if it disputed the claim in good faith. The claim is then arbitrated or litigated under the policy.
